say: You give it a triangle. It draws the **incircle**, the circle that fits inside and touches all three sides.
The key idea: the centre is where the **angle bisectors** meet, because that point is the same distance from every side.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level asked for it in 2024 (Paper 2, Q6(a), 15 marks): bisect two angles of a given triangle and mark the incircle.

example.question: Construct the incircle of the triangle $ABC$ with $|AB| = 8$ cm, $|BC| = 7$ cm and $|AC| = 5$ cm. Show all construction lines.

steps.title: Draw the triangle
steps.say: Draw $[AB]$ first. Then find $C$ with two arcs, so the sides are accurate.

lines.text: Draw $[AB]$ with $|AB| = 8$ cm.
With the compass point on $A$, draw an arc of radius $5$ cm.
With the compass point on $B$, draw an arc of radius $7$ cm. Where the arcs cross is $C$.
Join $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $C$.

steps.title: Bisect the angle at A
steps.say: The incentre lies on each angle bisector. Bisect the angle at $A$ using Construction 1.

lines.text: With the compass point on $A$, draw an arc that cuts $[AB]$ and $[AC]$.
Keep the same width. Put the point on each cut in turn and draw two arcs that cross inside the angle.
Draw a line from $A$ through the crossing point.

steps.title: Bisect the angle at B
steps.say: Do the same at $B$. The two bisectors meet at one point, the **incentre** $I$.

lines.text: Repeat the construction at $B$.
Label the point where the two bisectors cross $I$.
Two bisectors are enough. Leave all the arcs showing.

steps.title: Draw the incircle
steps.say: The circle must touch each side, so its radius is the shortest distance from $I$ to a side. Drop a perpendicular.

lines.text: From $I$, construct the perpendicular to $[AB]$ (Construction 5). Where it meets $[AB]$ is $T$.
With the compass point on $I$ and the pencil on $T$, draw the circle.
It touches all three sides.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: incircle with centre $I$, the meeting point of the angle bisectors

ordinary.tip: Bisect at least two angles. One correct bisector earns only partial credit, and a bisector with no arcs shown earns less.
Make sure the bisectors cross. If they do not meet, the incircle is not found and a mark is lost.
Even one correct arc is work of merit, so always start the construction and leave the arcs showing.

say: You give it a circle with centre $O$ and a point $P$ on it. It draws the **tangent** at $P$, a line that touches the circle only at $P$.
The key idea: a tangent is **perpendicular** to the radius at the point of contact, so you draw the radius $[OP]$ and then a perpendicular to it at $P$.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level papers 2015 to 2025 did not test it as a separate part, so it is a learn-and-know construction.

example.question: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $4$ cm. $P$ is a point on the circle. Construct the tangent to the circle at $P$.

steps.title: Draw the radius
steps.say: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at $P$. Draw the radius first.

lines.text: Draw the circle with centre $O$ and radius $4$ cm. Mark $P$ on it.
Draw the line from $O$ through $P$, and extend it past $P$.

steps.title: Mark two points either side
steps.say: Construction 4 draws a perpendicular to a line through a point on it. First mark two points the same distance from $P$.

lines.text: With the compass point on $P$, draw an arc that cuts the extended radius on both sides of $P$.
Call the two cuts $X$ and $Y$. Now $|PX| = |PY|$.

steps.title: Find the perpendicular
steps.say: Open the compass wider. Draw two arcs that cross above and below the line.

lines.text: With the compass point on $X$, draw an arc above the line and one below it.
Keep the same width. With the point on $Y$, draw arcs that cross the first two.
Mark the crossing points $U$ and $V$.

steps.title: Draw the tangent
steps.say: Join $U$ and $V$. This line passes through $P$ at a right angle to $[OP]$, so it is the **tangent**.

lines.text: With the straight edge, draw the line $UV$ through $P$.
Label it $t$. It touches the circle at $P$ only.

say: You give it a triangle. It finds the **centroid** $G$, the balance point where the three medians meet.
The key idea: a median runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, and the centroid sits two thirds of the way along it. On coordinates, it is the average of the vertices.

how.higher: Higher level asked for it as a construction in 2015 (Paper 2, Q6(a), 5 marks) and 2024 (Paper 2, Q4(a), 15 marks), then a proof about the medians.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asked for it in 2025 (Paper 2, Q9(a), 15 marks): construct a midpoint and find the centroid, with measurements.

example.question: The triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1, 2)$, $B(7, 4)$ and $C(4, 9)$. Find the midpoint $D$ of $[BC]$, then find the centroid $G$ of the triangle.

steps.title: Find the midpoint D
steps.say: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Average the coordinates of $B$ and $C$ to find $\hl{1}{D}$.

lines.text: So $\hl{1}{D} = \left(\frac{11}{2}, \frac{13}{2}\right)$. The median is $[AD]$.

steps.title: Use the 2 to 1 ratio
steps.say: The centroid $\hl{2}{G}$ is two thirds of the way from $A$ to $D$. Find the $x$-coordinate first.

steps.title: Check with the average
steps.say: A quick check: the centroid is the average of the three vertices.

lines.text: Both methods agree. $\hl{2}{G} = (4, 5)$.

higher.tip: Show the construction. Marks go for finding midpoints, and a median drawn with nothing shown earns less.
Find the midpoint of at least two sides. Two midpoints is a mid-credit step on its own.
Draw at least one full median. It is a high-credit step, and the centroid is where the medians meet.

ordinary.tip: Construct the midpoint with arcs. A correct midpoint is worth most of the first step.
Write down any measurement you use, such as the length of a median or a part of it. A relevant measurement written earns credit even if the rest is wrong.

say: You give it a statement or an argument. It uses the right word for each part: **theorem**, **proof**, **axiom**, **corollary**, **converse**, **implies**.
The key idea: the **converse** swaps the two halves of "if … then …". The converse of a true statement can be false.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it as short true or false parts with a reason (Paper 2, Q6 in 2022 and 2023, 10 marks): is a statement about triangles or a parallelogram true, and why.

example.question: Statement: "If $x = 3$, then $x^2 = 9$." (a) Write down the converse. (b) Is the converse true or false? Give a reason.

steps.title: Write the converse
steps.say: The statement has the form "if $P$ then $Q$". The **converse** swaps them: "if $Q$ then $P$".

lines.text: Converse: "If $x^2 = 9$, then $x = 3$."

steps.title: Test the converse
steps.say: To show a statement false you need only one example where it fails. Solve $\hl{1}{x^2 = 9}$ and see if $x = 3$ is the only answer.

steps.title: Give the reason
steps.say: The value $\hl{2}{x = -3}$ makes $x^2 = 9$ true but $x = 3$ false. That is a counterexample.

lines.text: So the converse is **false**.
Reason: $x = -3$ gives $x^2 = 9$, but $x \neq 3$.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: Converse: if $x^2 = 9$ then $x = 3$. It is **false**, since $x = -3$ is a counterexample.

ordinary.tip: Give a reason as well as True or False. A correct tick with no reason earns only low partial credit.

sources.quote: Correct box (True) ticked but no work

ordinary.tip: Use the properties of the shape in your reason, for example the sides of a parallelogram being parallel and equal.
